subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Randomized Controlled Trials in Policy
description: A quick, practical guide to Randomized Controlled Trials in Policy.

hook.text: A city tested two letters: one with social norms, one without. The norm letter increased recycling by 12%.

buildup.text: RCTs randomly assign people to treatment and control groups. The comparison reveals the true effect of the intervention.

discovery.text: Before nudge units, most policies were designed by intuition. RCTs bring evidence-based rigor.

twist.text: Many intuitive interventions fail RCTs. Scary health warnings sometimes backfire, increasing risky behavior through.

climax.text: RCTs protect against wishful thinking. Testing before national rollout saves money and avoids harmful surprises.

punchline.text: Test a policy before you scale it. Good intentions are not enough.

quiz.question: Why are RCTs important in behavioral policy?
options: They always confirm that nudges work
They reveal true effects by comparing treatment and control groups
They eliminate the need for behavioral theory

details.summary: Randomized controlled trials in policy test behavioral interventions scientifically by randomly assigning citizens to treatment and control groups. This gold-standard method reveals what actually works rather than what policymakers assume should work.
details.whyItMatters: RCTs transformed behavioral policy from theory to evidence-based practice. By rigorously testing interventions before scaling, governments avoid wasting resources on interventions that sound good but fail to change behavior in practice.
takeaways: RCTs are the gold standard for testing whether behavioral interventions work
Random assignment isolates the causal effect of the intervention
Many intuitive-seeming interventions fail when properly tested

faq.question: Why are RCTs important for behavioral policy?
faq.answer: Because intuition about what changes behavior is often wrong. Many promising-sounding interventions have no effect when rigorously tested. RCTs prevent governments from scaling costly programs that do not actually improve outcomes.

faq.question: Are there ethical concerns with testing policies on citizens?
faq.answer: Some argue that randomly giving different citizens different policy experiences is unfair. Proponents counter that implementing an untested policy universally is more ethically risky than testing it first on a small scale to verify it actually helps.
